title: the Gut Microbiome as a Disease Modifier of Heterotopic Ossification
text:
Heterotopic ossification is the process of abnormal bone formation in soft tissues and is caused by genetic
mutations and musculoskeletal trauma, both of which involve inflammation. Commensal microbiota can regulate
inflammation in mouse and human hosts. This proposal will determine whether commensal microbiota contribute
to HO and potentially define a new mechanism by which to control heterotopic ossification.

title: Length, methylation, and purity of expanded C9orf72 repeat across diseases, tissues, and cell populations
text:
To unravel the clinical variability seen in people with a repeat expansion in a gene called C9orf72, we will use a
pioneering sequencing technology that enables us to accurately capture this expansion. We will examine people
with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), as well as people without any
symptoms of these devastating diseases. Our study has been designed to reveal whether the length,
methylation, and/or purity of the expansion may have the ability to modify these diseases.

title: Leveraging Causal Machine Learning Methods to Enhance Tobacco Control Interventions
text:
This study aims to employ innovative modeling approaches to advance our understanding of e-cigarette use
uptake and explore potential causal pathways leading to this behavior among youth and young adults. The
findings from this project could be used to inform tobacco-related interventions and communications strategies.

title: Development and Validation of a Novel AI-Augmented Mobile Platform for Early Head Shape Screening in Infants.
text:
Early detection of craniosynostosis enables minimally invasive surgery that improves neurodevelopmental
outcomes and reduces healthcare costs, yet delayed diagnosis remains common in primary care. This project
will develop and validate CranioSure, a mobile, AI-enabled screening tool that uses standard photographs to
detect craniosynostosis with accuracy comparable to CT imaging but without radiation, cost, or referral delays.
By enabling timely, accessible, and accurate diagnosis in primary care settings, CranioSure has the potential to
reduce morbidity, expand access to optimal surgical care, and lower the national healthcare burden.

title: Dynamic Brain Imaging of Speech in Primary Progressive Aphasia
text:
Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurological disorder characterized by progressive decline of speech
and language. We propose to examine neural oscillations in different variants of PPA using high temporal
resolution imaging with magnetoencephalography. The results of the proposed studies will identify some of the
earliest functional manifestations of brain network dysfunction in PPA variants that will allow us to identify
putative brain network targets for behavioral or neuromodulation therapies.

title: Achieving enhanced cytosolic delivery and greater efficacy of therapeutic nucleic acids using DNA-surfactant conjugates
text:
Therapeutic nucleic acids (TNAs) have the potential to change the way we treat disease, however roughly 90%
of TNAs delivered into cells never make it past the initial cellular entry and endocytosis pathway and remain in
endosomes where they are degraded, resulting in significant waste and limiting efficacy. The work proposed
here utilizes a TNA delivery platform known as a nucleic acid nanocapsule (NAN) which can release membrane
disrupting DNA surfactant conjugates (DSCs) in endosomes as a way to enhance the cytosolic delivery of TNAs.
The research objectives proposed here aims to study how the chemical structure of DSCs can be tuned to
enhance cytosolic delivery, while also investigating ways to target these DSCs to specific cell types, and to
investigate how the lessons learned from this system can be applied to other therapeutic modalities that suffer
from limited endosomal escape or combined with TNAs to achieve synergistic therapeutic outcomes.

title: Core 06: Biomedical Informatics Core
text: The overall goal of the Biomedical Informatics (BMI) Core of the Louisiana Clinical and Translational Science Center (LA CaTS) is to build on our accomplishments and continue to develop and deploy “state of the art” informatics services to LA CaTS investigators. During the current funding period, the BMI Core provided significant support to 27 LA CaTS Investigators across 14 institutions, resulting in 46 publications and 18 funded grant applications. The BMI Core constructed 12 “virtual cohorts”, which were used in 30 projects leading to 3 major NCI grant awards. We created the data infrastructure for 3 “virtual biorepositories” and provided the informatics backbone for the participation of LA CaTS in the NIH “All of Us” research program.. The BMI Core contributed to the LA CaTS response to the pandemic in multiple ways: 1) Supported 2 multi-CTR N3C projects exploring the relationship of drug exposures and rurality with disease outcomes; 2) Provided the informatics infrastructure for 2 epidemiological studies; and 3) Supported 3 projects on variant sequencing in Louisiana. The BMI Core also supported the COBRE Center for Translational Viral Oncology and served an invaluable role in the close collaboration between LA CaTS and the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB)-led Center for Clinical and Translational Sciences (CCTS. Our commitment to building a robust pipeline of translational data scientists led to a) the first Master of Science program in Bioinformatics in Louisiana, and b) the expansion of Core personnel to include 3 early-stage investigators. During the next funding period, the BMI Core will expand its mission to include integrative clinical and bioinformatics, machine learning/artificial intelligence, access to national and regional clinical databases, individualized mentorship, didactics, as well as community stakeholder and citizen scientist support. In cycle 3 we will pursue three important specific aims. Specific Aim 1. Provide training and enhance utilization of high-resolution bioinformatics and artificial intelligence/machine learning algorithms. Specific Aim 2: Expand our existing support for collaboration and data sharing within LA CaTS Cores and between LA CaTS investigators and CTSA Centers, as well as with Centers of Biomedical Research Excellence (COBRE) and the Louisiana Biomedical Research Network (LBRN) by broadening the geographic scope and population coverage of data resources available to LA CaTS investigators. Specific Aim 3: Expand our educational mission, in close cooperation with the Professional Development (PD) Core, to recruit and create a pipeline of translational data scientists and to enable and support data research by citizen scientists and community stakeholders. We expect that the accomplishment of these Aims will produce a cutting edge, multidisciplinary BMI Core that forms the data science backbone of the LA CaTS Center and enables local, regional, and national collaborations, while enhancing our data scientist pipeline and public awareness. The BMI Core will give a vital contribution to the Center’s mission to transform and grow clinical and translational research in Louisiana.

title: Improving External Validity of the RECHARGE Trial through a Partially Randomized Patient Preference Framework
text:
We will enroll 1,000 women and 1,000 Black or Hispanic patients who are eligible but decline randomization in
the RECHARGE (REvascularization CHoices Among under-Represented Groups Evaluation) randomized
clinical trials (RCTs) comparing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and percutaneous coronary intervention
(PCI) in a parallel observational cohort. This will establish a partially randomized patient preference (PRPP)
framework to enhance the generalizability of RCT findings to the broader eligible population. We will collect
detailed baseline characteristics, document reasons for declining randomization and preference-related factors,
and conduct follow-up in parallel with the randomized cohort.

title: Engineering programmable enzymes for proteome editing
text:
The ability to label, modify, and manipulate endogenous proteins would enable a wide range of applications in
biology and biomedicine. This research plan describes the development of modular molecular architectures for
devising programmable enzymes for such purposes. A successful completion of this proposal will establish
transformative technologies with exceptional generality, modularity, and flexibility for reprogramming the
proteome.

title: Role of LGR+ connective tissue progenitors in TMJ development
text:
Disorders of the temporomandibular joint of the jaw are a common source of chronic pain. This
proposal uses complementary zebrafish and mouse models to investigate the role of LGRs, which
potentiate Wnt signaling, in maintaining and controlling differentiation of stem cells that give rise
to diverse jaw joint connective tissues. Knowledge gained from these studies will inform future
studies aimed at repairing and restoring damaged connective tissues in temporomandibular joint
disease.

title: 3-D biofabricated feto-maternal interface tissue model to determine drug efficacy during pregnancy to reduce the risk of preterm birth
text:
To overcome the limitations of no existing drugs against preterm birth as well as challenges in conducting
clinical trials during pregnancy, we will develop an in vitro model: a 3D bioprinted feto-maternal interface (part
of uterine tissue) tissue chip that can model the disease state of pregnancy. In collaboration with the National
Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS), the tissue chip model capable of conducting high-
throughput screening of drug libraries will be utilized to test up to 1,000 drug compounds for their usefulness in
treating pregnant women and their fetuses and for testing potential adverse effects of the drug compounds.
Successful development of this high-throughput model will allow testing of many drugs currently in use for
other clinical indications, but not for pregnant women due to uncertainty of their adverse effects on pregnancy,
as well as initiating discovery of new drugs that can reduce the risk of preterm birth.

title: FOXE3 in Creating Lens Chromatin Architecture and Transcriptional Identity
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health, because a molecular understanding of how transcription
factors function cooperatively to regulate genomic epigenetic landscapes lies at the heart of curative and
regenerative disease therapies. The ocular lens, with its uniquely simple, isolated architecture and stereotypical
patterns of continuous growth and differentiation provides a powerful model system to uncover the fundamental
rules of transcriptional control that govern development, structure and function of diverse tissues and organs.
The proposed research is relevant to the NIH’s mission because mutations in FOXE3 cause a wide variety of
ocular abnormalities, yet the mechanism(s) by which FOXE3 controls gene expression remain(s) almost entirely
unknown.

title: Enhancing Cancer Immunotherapy for Refractory High-Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer with Novel Platinum Nanotherapeutics
text:
High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is the deadliest gynecological cancer in the United States, with
approximately 80% of women experiencing relapse due to resistance to chemotherapy and immunotherapy. This
proposal aims to develop novel immunogenic nanomedicines that kill therapeutic-resistant HGSOC cells,
reprogram the tumor microenvironment, and enhance cancer immunotherapy. If successful, this innovative
approach could validate a new treatment option for refractory HGSOC patients with limited alternatives,
ultimately improving their survival rates.

title: Cancer Population Sciences
text: CANCER POPULATION SCIENCES (CPS) The Cancer Population Sciences (CPS) Program brings together 50 faculty, representing 12 departments at Dartmouth’s Geisel School of Medicine (Geisel), Dartmouth Health (DH) and the White River Junction VT Veterans Administration Medical Center (VA), with research interests relevant to the three central CPS Program themes: 1) Life Course Cancer Epidemiology; 2) Health Care Delivery Science; and 3) Methodological Advances in Population Sciences. By bringing together scientists studying cancer risk, those addressing risk behaviors, those developing innovative methodologies, and those designing and evaluating cancer care delivery and policy, CPS Program Members seek to control cancer and improve population health within our catchment area and beyond. The CPS Program’s Specific Aims are to: 1) Conduct population-based studies to understand the molecular, behavioral, and environmental basis of cancer occurrence and outcomes across the life course; 2) Establish a scientific basis for policies and practices that improve cancer screening, quality of care delivery, and health outcomes across the cancer continuum, from prevention to survivorship; and 3) Design, test, and implement interventions and promote policies that reduce cancer risk and cancer burden in our catchment area, nationally, and beyond. Peer-reviewed cancer-relevant research direct cost support currently totals $11.6M, a 33% increase from 2019, with NCI funding representing $1.9M. Fifteen (15) CPS Program Members currently have a total of 21 CCSG-defined R01-equivalent awards. Since 2019, the Program has 703 cancer-related publications: 26% intra-programmatic, 12% inter-programmatic, 24% with investigators from other NCI cancer centers, and 20% in high-impact journals (i.e., impact factor ≥10, and/or Altmetric >95th percentile). These percentages are comparable to 2019 values (31% intra-programmatic, 9% inter-programmatic, 20% high- impact). CPS Program leaders work closely with the DCC Triple Helix Workgroup, consisting of the Offices of Cancer Research Training and Education Coordination (CRTEC) and Community Outreach and Engagement (COE), to pursue catchment-relevant research, community outreach and engagement, and contribution to education and career development. DCC support for faculty recruitment and development enhances the CPS Program’s ability to promote and convene a campus-wide cancer workforce. DCC institutional Developmental Funding (“Prouty Pilot grants”) and usage of DCC shared resources accelerate CPS Program Members toward extramural NCI and other cancer-relevant funding. Aligned with DCC’s Strategic Plan to Accelerate the Translational Pipeline, CPS Program leaders have defined specific plans for future growth that will advance DCC’s strategic scientific priorities of Precision Cancer Prevention, Next-Generation Immunotherapies, and Innovation and Entrepreneurship.

title: Molecular mechanisms of pathway choice in DNA double strand break repair
text:
DNA double strand breaks are a dangerous, yet common form of DNA damage and their repair is essential
for cell survival. In humans, two major pathways rejoin broken chromosomes and the improper utilization of
these pathways is associated with the onset of cancer. Using advanced single-molecule imaging in a
physiological cell-free extract, this proposal will elucidate the mechanisms by which DNA double strand
break repair pathways are selected.

title: A novel AR degrader in castrate-resistant prostate cancer
text:
The goal of this application is to test the therapeutic efficacy of novel therapeutic agents for AR
protein degradation using autophagy-targeting chimera (AUTOTAC) in castrate-resistant
prostate cancer.

title: Acquisition of molecular characterization instrumentation to advance mass spectrometry capabilities for research and teaching at America's Arctic University
text:
This proposal seeks to acquire an ultrahigh pressure liquid chromatography triple quadrupole mass
spectrometer (UHPLC-MS/MS) that will enhance biomedical and critical arctic based research, and support
local teaching capacity, at the University of Alaska Fairbanks (UAF). UAF is the largest research University in
Alaska, but lacks instrumentation to provide hands-on training for graduate and undergraduate biomedical and
chemistry students in modern analytical techniques to meet workforce demands, or to support significant
research needs for cutting edge Arctic research. Acquisition of a UHPLC-MS/MS will directly support a broad
range of UAF researchers who study unique biomedical models of hibernation and endurance exercise in the
Arctic, as well as critical teaching needs in the chemistry department.

title: Robust Mass Spectrometric Protein/Peptide Assays for Type 1 Diabetes Clinical Applications
text:
The proposed research aims to develop highly specific, reproducible, and transferable multiplex targeted mass
spectrometry assays to enable accurate monitoring of isoform-specific markers of endocrine and exocrine
functions in type 1 diabetes (T1D) clinical research. These assays if developed successfully will make a
significant contribution to more precise monitoring of pancreatic endocrine and exocrine function, the disease
progression, as well as the efficacy of clinical interventions in T1D patients.

title: Targeting CAMKK2 for the treatment of advanced prostate cancer
text:
Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men and is often resistant to current treatments.
This project will use mouse models to study how a protein called CAMKK2 promotes the spread of prostate
cancer, and impairs the immune system, while testing new drugs that block CAMKK2 activity to see if they can
slow cancer growth and make the immune system more effective in attacking the tumor. If successful, this
research could lead to new treatment options and improve outcomes for men with advanced prostate cancer.

title: Chemistry and Biology of Assembly-Line Polyketide Synthases
text:
Assembly-line polyketide synthases are very large catalytic machines responsible for the biosynthesis of
structurally complex and diverse natural products including many antibiotics. The goal of our research is to
advance our understanding of the structure and mechanism of these remarkable enzymes, and to learn how
to engineer new assembly-line synthases. We also seek to understand the biological role of an unusual
polyketide natural product made principally by certain bacteria that cause nocardiosis infections.
